Which cave the title means is canvassed by four of them and dismissed by one. Keil and Delitzsch take the definite article to point either to the cave of Adullam or to that of Engedi, and describe the second as opening from a narrow concealed entrance into so labyrinthine a maze of passages and vaults that the torches and lines of explorers have not to this day reached its extremities. Adam Clarke reviews the two occasions and judges Engedi the likelier if the inscription can be depended on, adding that were the title doubtful he should refer the psalm instead to the captives in Babylon. John Calvin also prefers the second cave and adds a qualification about the composition: the psalm is a recollection of the substance of the prayers offered there, since it cannot be supposed that he had any opportunity of writing at the time. Matthew Henry says the question is not material, since it is plain he was in distress. Adam Clarke then rejects a bishop who entitled the psalm a prayer of the Messiah taken and deserted: it may be so, he says, but where is the evidence, except in a conjectural system.

Whether the voice was audible in that cave divides them further. John Gill argues that it was, since the cave was large enough to hold six hundred men without their being seen and to let them talk without being heard, so the prayer might well have been spoken aloud. C.H. Spurgeon agrees for a different reason, that in the loneliness of the place he could use his voice as much as he pleased and made its gloomy vaults echo with his appeals. Matthew Henry takes the opposite view, that being hidden he dared not speak audibly lest it betray him, and answers that mental prayer is vocal to God, who hears the groanings that cannot be uttered. Augustine of Hippo sets the question aside: many cry to the Lord not with their own voice but with the voice of their body, and unless a man cries with lungs and tongue his neighbour does not hear him, but his thought is his cry to the Lord. He presses the same point on the next clause, since to pour out a prayer before God is to pour it where he alone sees.

What the pouring out excludes is Calvin’s subject. John Calvin makes it the reverse of two opposite faults, of the perplexing anxieties which men brood over inwardly until they torture themselves, and of the frantic exclamations of those who find no comfort in providence: the psalmist neither gave way before men to loud and senseless lamentation nor let himself be tormented by suppressed cares. He adds that only such prayer can explain the restraint, since hemmed in on every side it was scarcely possible to spare so implacable an enemy without being fortified by it. Matthew Henry draws the same distinction toward the reader: we are apt to show our trouble too much to ourselves, aggravating it and poring upon it, which does us no service, and we should allow no complaint to ourselves or others that we could not with sincerity make to God; complainants, he adds, must be suppliants. John Gill notes that the complaint is not of the Lord but of himself and of his own unbelief. C.H. Spurgeon watches the prayer take shape, the natural longing first and the ordered supplication after, and observes that true prayers may differ in their diction but not in their direction. Charles Ellicott renders the overwhelming of the spirit literally as a muffling upon him, so that the man was so wrapped in gloom that he could not see the path before him, and it is God, emphatically, who knew that path.

Whether the psalmist looked or commands us to look is disputed. John Gill reports that some render the verbs as imperatives, look on the right hand and behold, taking them either as spoken by the man to his own soul or as an address to God, and that one commentator went further and read them as addressed to the right hand of God itself; he rejects that, since looking cannot properly be ascribed to a hand and since the psalmist is not speaking to the Lord here but of men. Charles Ellicott takes the side Gill rejects: the received version follows the ancient versions in turning Hebrew imperatives into historic tenses, but the imperatives are easily intelligible if taken rhetorically, and the psalm loses in liveliness by missing them — look to the right and see, not a friend is in sight. John Wesley and Keil and Delitzsch both explain why the right hand is named, since that is where a patron or a friend would stand. Matthew Henry fills in the history, that when the fugitive looked for an advocate none would venture, one man’s help having already cost him his life and another’s nearly so, and adds that many good men have been deceived by such swallow-friends, who are gone when winter comes. Adam Clarke notes the application of the verse to a later desertion by disciples, and observes that a handful of men in a cave were nothing against a king and his army.

The word prison is where the entry turns on itself. John Gill denies both the readings he has met: it does not mean purgatory, to which some writers wrest the words very absurdly, nor the prison of the body, as a Jewish writer took it, but the cave in which he was detained, or rather the straits that pressed him on every side. Adam Clarke keeps it to the cave whose mouth the enemy held, and then gives his old Psalter, which takes the other view Gill rejects, praying that the soul be led out of the corruption of the body, which corruption is bodily pain in which the soul is in anguish. Keil and Delitzsch observe that this is the only passage in the whole Psalter where the poet calls the distress he is in a prison. Charles Ellicott takes that singularity a step further and turns it against the title: the expression must certainly be figurative of distress, and it was probably this word that gave rise to the inscription about the cave.

What the righteous do at the close is read four ways. Charles Ellicott notes that the verb is used in a hostile sense elsewhere and therefore prefers to follow the old Greek, so that in his case the righteous are waiting until God deals bountifully with him; the sense of waiting for, he adds, is favoured by the construction and by an old translator’s rendering of the same word in a proverb. Adam Clarke reads a third sense entirely, that they shall crown him, and suggests that on the death of the persecutor the pious would cheerfully join to make him king, being convinced that God intended it. John Wesley has them flock to him from all parts to rejoice and bless God with him and for him. Keil and Delitzsch take the clause as bringing the whole congregation of the righteous in to praise the divine name, and draw the conclusion that the poet does not after all find himself so absolutely alone as the earlier verse made it seem. Matthew Henry makes the two names of the fifth verse answer the two complaints, the refuge against the cave which was but a poor refuge and the portion against the crown which was but a poor portion, and observes that those who take the Lord for their God may humbly claim their interest in him.
